title: Iceberg features: evolution, time travel, row-level changes
summary: Hidden partitioning, partition and schema evolution, time travel, branches and tags, and the two strategies for updates and deletes.

blocks.text: Every feature in this chapter is a consequence of the metadata tree from chapter 22: files are tracked explicitly, columns have ids, and snapshots are kept until expired. Examples use Spark SQL with the Iceberg SQL extensions enabled and a catalog named `lake`.
23.1 Hidden partitioning and transforms

In Hive-style tables the partition is a column users must know about: you add `event_date` derived from `event_ts`, and a query filtering only on `event_ts` scans everything. Iceberg instead declares partitions as **transforms of source columns**. The spec records 'day of `event_ts`', writers compute it, and the planner converts a predicate on `event_ts` into a partition filter automatically. Users never see or write the partition value.

head: Transform
Spark DDL
Use for
rows: Time-series data; choose the grain that gives files of hundreds of MB per partition
High-cardinality keys: spreads rows over N hash buckets, helps joins and point lookups
Prefix grouping of strings, or ranges of integers

blocks.title: Spark SQL: hidden partitioning
blocks.text:
CREATE TABLE lake.sales.orders (
  order_id     BIGINT,
  customer_id  BIGINT,
  status       STRING,
  amount       DECIMAL(12,2),
  order_ts     TIMESTAMP)
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (days(order_ts), bucket(16, customer_id));

-- planner derives the day partition filter from order_ts
SELECT sum(amount) FROM lake.sales.orders
WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-01 00:00:00'
  AND order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2026-11-02 00:00:00';

Over-partitioning is the classic mistake: `hours(ts)` on a table that receives 2 GB a day produces 24 partitions of about 80 MB, each split into several small files by parallel writers. Partition for pruning on common filters and use sort order (chapter 25) for the rest.
23.2 Partition evolution

Because partitions are part of metadata, not of the directory layout, you can change the spec. Existing files keep the spec they were written with (each manifest records its spec id); new writes use the new spec. The planner evaluates the filter against each spec separately. No data is rewritten unless you choose to compact old files into the new layout.

blocks.title: Spark SQL: partition evolution

blocks.text: The default name of a field derived by `days(order_ts)` is `order_ts_day`; check the `partitions` or `files` metadata tables if unsure. In format v1, dropped fields remain in the spec as `void` transforms, which is one more reason to prefer v2 or later.
23.3 Schema evolution by field id
Every column has a unique integer field id, and data files store field ids alongside values. Readers map by id, not by name or position. That makes these changes metadata-only and safe:

items: **Add** a column: new id; old files simply have no values for it and read as null (or as the default value in v3).
**Drop** a column: the id is removed from the current schema; old values are ignored and the id is never reused.
**Rename**: only the name in the schema changes; files still match by id.
**Widen** types: int to long, float to double, increasing decimal precision. Narrowing or arbitrary type changes are not allowed.

blocks.text: Name-based formats get this wrong in subtle ways: drop column `x`, add a new column `x`, and a name-mapped reader resurrects the old values. Iceberg's ids prevent that. Files imported from Hive tables have no ids, so they need a name mapping (`schema.name-mapping.default`).
23.4 Time travel, rollback, branches and tags
Any snapshot still in metadata can be read. Rollback moves the `main` ref back to an older snapshot; it is a metadata commit and does not delete the newer files until they are expired.

blocks.title: Spark SQL: time travel and refs

blocks.text: A **tag** is a named, immutable pointer to one snapshot with its own retention, useful for month-end or regulatory states that must outlive normal snapshot expiry. A **branch** is a movable pointer with its own history. Writing to a branch (for example `INSERT INTO lake.sales.orders.branch_audit ...`, or the write-audit-publish session settings) lets a pipeline land data, run quality checks against the branch, and then fast-forward `main` to it with the `fast_forward` procedure. Readers of `main` never see unchecked data. Exact procedure names and options change between releases: check the current documentation.

blocks.title: Write-audit-publish for a finance table
blocks.text: The finance gold table must never expose a load that fails reconciliation. The nightly job writes into branch `audit`, runs row-count and sum checks against `VERSION AS OF 'audit'`, and only on success fast-forwards `main`. On failure the branch is dropped and on-call is paged; dashboards keep showing yesterday's consistent state.
23.5 Row-level changes: copy-on-write vs merge-on-read

Files are immutable, so an UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE must either rewrite the affected files or record which rows are no longer valid. Iceberg supports both, chosen per operation with the table properties `write.delete.mode`, `write.update.mode` and `write.merge.mode`.

head: Copy-on-write (COW)
Merge-on-read (MOR)
rows: Rewrite every data file containing a changed row
Write new rows plus delete files marking old rows
High: changing 1 row in a 512 MB file rewrites 512 MB
Readers apply deletes at scan time until compaction
Batch updates touching large fractions of files, read-heavy tables
Frequent small updates, CDC, GDPR deletes

blocks.text: Delete file types

items: **Position deletes** (v2): rows identified by data file path plus row position. Precise and cheap to apply, but the writer must first find the rows, which Spark does during the MERGE scan.

**Equality deletes** (v2): rows identified by column values, for example `order_id = 981`. The writer needs no read, which suits streaming CDC (Flink commonly uses them), but every reader must compare these keys against all older data files: expensive until compacted.

**Deletion vectors** (v3): a bitmap of deleted positions per data file stored in a Puffin file, with at most one vector per data file in a snapshot. They replace position delete files for v3 tables and keep the number of delete artifacts bounded.

blocks.title: Spark SQL: CDC upsert with merge-on-read
blocks.text:
ALTER TABLE lake.sales.orders SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'write.merge.mode'  = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.update.mode' = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.delete.mode' = 'merge-on-read');

MERGE INTO lake.sales.orders t
USING staging.order_changes s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'D' THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'D' THEN INSERT *;

`UPDATE SET *` and `INSERT *` match columns by name, so the source must contain every target column. Deduplicate the source to one row per key first (latest change wins), or the MERGE fails because several source rows match one target row.

blocks.title: Choose a strategy for three tables
blocks.text: Pick partition transforms and a row-level change mode for: (a) a 20 TB clickstream table queried by event time and occasionally purged per user for GDPR; (b) a 50 GB customer dimension updated by hourly CDC with about 1% of rows changing per day; (c) a 2 TB ledger rewritten monthly when an accounting period is restated. Justify each choice by write cost, read cost and maintenance.
hints: How many files does a typical change touch in each case?
Who reads each table, and how sensitive are they to scan-time delete application?
What compaction would each merge-on-read choice require?

items: Partitions are transforms of source columns; queries filter on real columns and the planner derives partition filters.
Partition specs can evolve; old files keep their spec, new files use the new one, nothing is rewritten.
Schema evolution is safe because files and schemas match columns by field id, not by name.
Snapshots enable time travel and rollback; tags pin states, branches enable write-audit-publish.
Copy-on-write pays at write time, merge-on-read pays at read time until compaction.
Position deletes, equality deletes and v3 deletion vectors differ in who pays the cost of finding rows.

blocks.q: A table is partitioned by `days(event_ts)`. An analyst writes `WHERE event_ts > now() - INTERVAL 2 HOURS`. What happens?
options: Pruning works only if the table is also sorted by event_ts
Full scan, because the filter does not mention the partition column
The query fails until the analyst adds an event_day filter
The planner derives the matching day partitions from the predicate on event_ts and prunes the rest
blocks.explain: Hidden partitioning maps predicates on the source column through the transform. Needing an explicit partition column filter is the Hive-style behaviour Iceberg removes.

blocks.q: You change a table from `days(ts)` to `hours(ts)`. What happens to the existing two years of data?
options: It keeps the daily spec; new writes use hourly; queries plan across both specs
It is rewritten into hourly partitions during the ALTER
It is moved to a new table location
blocks.explain: Partition evolution is metadata-only. Each manifest records its spec id, so both layouts coexist. Rewriting is optional, done later by compaction if useful.

blocks.q: A Flink CDC job writes equality deletes every minute. Queries slow down week by week. Why?
options: Equality deletes physically rewrite data files on every commit
Equality deletes must be matched by value against all older data files at read time, and they accumulate until compaction
Equality deletes are only allowed in format v1
blocks.explain: Equality deletes are cheap to write because the writer does not look up rows; the reader pays by joining keys against older data. Without regular compaction the cost grows. They are a v2 feature and never rewrite data files.

blocks.q: Which mechanism best lets a pipeline validate a load before any `main` reader can see it?
options: Writing to a branch, auditing it, then fast-forwarding main
A tag created after the load
Time travel with TIMESTAMP AS OF
Rolling back after a failed check
blocks.explain: A branch isolates the new snapshots from main until published. A tag is an immutable pointer, and rollback only fixes things after readers may already have seen bad data.
